extracted.intended_audience: amateur and professional astronomers observing meteor showers (Perseids) and readers/students of physiological oddities
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and criteria for observing, recording, and analyzing the August (Perseid) meteor shower — how to count meteors, record tracks/streaks, determine radiants, and control observational variables. The page also contains field-observation criteria and diagnostic features for the folkloric/medical phenomenon called 'Jumpers'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Momentary character of the 'Jumpers' phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The acts of the Jumper — striking, throwing, dropping, crying, jerking, or jumping — are momentary: 'In but a second or so all the acts ... are over completely, and he is about in the same condition as before he was surprised.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with trance/hysteria where manifestations may last minutes to hours or days; the Jumper's explosion is sudden and the subject is at once ready for a new explosion on proper excitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence/permanence of liability in 'Jumpers'
rubrics_metrics.description: After the habit of jumping is formed the subject 'is yet always capable of displaying the phenomena in a greater or less degree at any moment: once a Jumper, always a Jumper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike epidemic jerking/rolling or transient hysteria, the liability in Jumpers is long-lasting and can be observed across years and generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary nature of Jumping
rubrics_metrics.description: Jumping is described as 'fully as hereditary as insanity, or epilepsy, or hay-fever,' with family clusters and multi-generation traces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field observations (multiple cases in the same families) are used to support heredity; genealogical tracing back decades is recommended to assess inheritance patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endemic and psycho-contagious distribution (Jumpers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jumping seems to be 'endemic, confined mainly to the north woods of Maine and to those of French descent, and is psycho-contagious — that is, can be caught by personal contact, like chorea and hysteria.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare occurrences across regions/races; note that similar phenomena have been reported (e.g., among Malays), suggesting distributional/contagional study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin hypothesis: evolution from tickling (Jumpers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jumping is probably an evolution of tickling: teasing, tickling, and startling in leisure may, by mental contagion, practice, and inheritance, ripen into the malady.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theory is presented as consistent with physiology and as an explanatory hypothesis to be weighed against alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to observer error and fraud when studying human phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The six sources of error that are involved in all experiments with human beings were not fully eliminated ... that the Jumpers ... experimented with me, and not I with the Jumpers ... victims of intentional or unintentional fraud.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain skepticism; explicitly identify and attempt to eliminate common human-subject experimental errors and the possibility of deliberate or inadvertent deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific observer must record notable features for later comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific observer 'zealously endeavors to record its more remarkable features ... remembering that his notes must hereafter have some value in the general comparison of results.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep diligent, systematic notes intended for aggregation and comparative analysis across observers and years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize observation hours for comparing hourly (horary) counts
rubrics_metrics.description: A fair comparison cannot be instituted between the horary numbers found by observers, unless the observations ... are made, in each case, at similar hours of the night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because meteor incidence varies through the night (often scarce in evening, more plentiful after midnight/morning), comparisons require observations taken at equivalent night hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer morning hours for Perseid observations
rubrics_metrics.description: The August Perseids 'are always best observable in the morning hours' and 'the most favorable time for such observations is in the morning hours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers should extend vigils into the morning when practicable; example: in one watch the rate before 11h was 47 and rose to about 80 in the last half of the watch; aggregate counts (e.g., 354 meteors during a long vigil) show strong morning increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for weather and moonlight in intensity comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little variation in intensity of annual returns 'when the conditions of weather and moonlight are fully taken into account.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always record and control for cloud cover, transparency, and moon phase/brightness when comparing shower intensities between years or observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use luminous streaks to register directions and fix radiants
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical feature is the streaks which frequently mark Perseid meteors and serve 'an extremely useful purpose in enabling the directions to be registered with great accuracy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streaks (phosphorescent lines) remain for about 1–4 seconds (writer's average 1.8s) and are the 'authentic signature' allowing the observer to fix beginning and ending points and thus map paths accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require a large number of accurately recorded tracks to determine the radiant
rubrics_metrics.description: The radiant 'must rest upon a large number of accurately recorded tracts, which intersect (on being prolonged backward) at a well-defined position.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate many high-quality tracks; radiants derived from large trustworthy samples (multiple observers/stations) are reliable and reproducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep nightly and hourly data separate to detect radiant displacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers should 'keep the data obtained each night separate' and 'the radiant point should be ascertained during each hour of observation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording per-hour radiants and maintaining nightly separation will reveal progressive shifts of the radiant (its apparent movement) and allow characterization of its extent and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for observer differences (vision, method, position) when comparing counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in vision, modes of observation, and in position must obviously affect the numbers to no small degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note observers' visual acuity, observing techniques, and geographic/positional differences; incorporate these variances or standardize methods when aggregating data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misassigning meteors from bordering showers to the Perseids
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent diffuseness of the radiant point is often brought about by ... allotting the meteors of bordering showers to the radiant of the Perseids, when in fact they belong to evidently distinct families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify meteors carefully by their path/radiant; separate minor/contemporary showers east of Perseus to avoid contamination of Perseid statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical caution: small samples and short series are unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Schmidt's figures are very small and much below numbers found in recent years; 'the averages in the table are not thoroughly reliable, inasmuch as they are based upon only a few years' observations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer longer series and larger samples; be wary of drawing conclusions from brief or scant observational records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map observed paths on prepared star-maps for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed paths were 'projected on the star-maps prepared by Professor Herschel' for purposes of luminous meteor committee analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standardized star-maps for plotting paths and sharing records; projection onto consistent charts facilitates cross-observer comparison and radiant derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseid physical characteristics to inform observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The theoretical velocity of these meteors is thirty-eight miles per second; they are among the swiftest class and most bright members show visible streaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given their high speed, rely on streaks rather than attempting to trace endpoints by eye; brighter meteors often show color variations (pale-green, orange) and are more likely to exhibit streaks useful for direction measurement.
